title: FRM Operational, Lesson 11: Cyber risk and technology resilience
subtitle: The one operational risk category with an active adversary trying to get past your controls
whyItMatters: Most operational risk comes from unintentional mistakes. Cyber is different in kind because there is an intelligent adversary who learns and adapts to the very defences you put up - which is why models built on historical frequency are especially weak here.
openingQuestion: Why do models built on historical loss frequency work so badly for cyber risk?
openingOptions: Because an active adversary keeps changing the method of attack
Because cyber attacks cause no financial damage, so there is nothing to record as a loss
Because supervisors prohibit the use of quantitative models for technology risk
Because the frequency of cyber attacks is a constant that does not change from year to year
explanation: For an earthquake or a keying error, the past is a reasonable guide to the future because the mechanism producing them does not change. An attacker watches your defences and moves somewhere else - the risk distribution shifts in response to the very act of defending.

diagram.label: Prevent: least privilege, network segmentation, patching
Respond and recover: rehearsed playbooks, segregated backups

realWorldExample.company: Concentration risk through shared technology providers
realWorldExample.description: The global financial industry depends increasingly on a small number of cloud and core software providers. Supervisors in several countries have raised the concern that this creates a common point of failure: one incident at one provider could disrupt many institutions simultaneously, turning an operational risk carried by each firm into a systemic risk for the whole sector.

quiz.question: What is the principle of least privilege designed to limit?
options: The number of staff who need to be given access accounts at all
The extent of the damage once an account has been compromised
The software licensing cost the organisation pays every year
The time it takes to restore data after an outage has occurred
quiz.explanation: The underlying assumption is that sooner or later an account will be taken over. Least privilege does not prevent that; it decides how far the attacker can travel afterwards, which is the difference between a minor incident and a system-wide breach. It does not reduce the number of accounts - everyone still gets one, just with narrower rights - and it has no bearing on licence costs or on how quickly data can be restored, which is a function of backup design rather than of access rights.

quiz.question: Why do backups need to be fully segregated from the main network?
options: Because regulation forbids holding backup data and source data on one type of device
Because backup data would take up too much of the primary system's storage capacity
Because modern ransomware seeks out and encrypts the backups too if they sit on the same network
Because backups are only ever needed in the event of a physical disaster at the site
quiz.explanation: A backup on a network drive that the primary servers can reach gets encrypted at the same moment as everything else. The common rule is to keep at least one copy that cannot be overwritten and is disconnected physically or logically from the operating network. Storage capacity is a cost question rather than a design constraint, no regulation dictates device types, and treating backups as a disaster-recovery measure alone is exactly the assumption ransomware was built to exploit.

quiz.question: What makes third-party risk a distinctive challenge in cyber security?
options: Third-party risk only arises when the entire technology stack is outsourced
Third parties always maintain higher security standards so no assessment is needed
A contract with a third party automatically transfers all legal responsibility to them
The firm bears the consequences of weaknesses in a system it does not control
quiz.explanation: Handing an activity to a provider does not hand over the responsibility owed to customers and to supervisors. The practical difficulty is assessing the security of a system you are not allowed to inspect, so you fall back on certifications, third-party audits and contractual terms. Outsourcing does not have to be total for the exposure to exist - a single payments interface is enough - and no contract shifts regulatory accountability, whatever the indemnity clauses say.

quiz.question: Why must a cyber incident response plan be rehearsed rather than only written?
options: Because only a rehearsal exposes dependencies that no document records
Because supervisors require at least two rehearsals in every financial year
Because a written plan expires unless it is updated each quarter
Because staff will not read the plan unless attendance is made compulsory
quiz.explanation: A rehearsal is where you discover that the standby system needs a password only one person knows, or that the emergency contact list is stored on the very system that has just been locked. Those dependencies are not written down anywhere, which is exactly why walking through the document cannot find them. Plans do need updating and staff do need to read them, but neither of those is the reason for the exercise - both could be satisfied by a plan that still fails on the night.

quiz.question: Why does detecting an intrusion matter as much as preventing one?
options: Because preventive measures usually cost a great deal more than detective ones
The attacker will get in, so the time to detection decides the damage
Because supervisors assess detection capability and nothing else
Because a detection system can automatically block every attack it has identified
quiz.explanation: No perimeter is airtight, so the question is not whether an intruder gets in but how long it takes to notice. The dwell time an attacker spends inside undetected is close to proportional to the eventual size of the loss, because that time is spent locating valuable data and reaching the backups. Detection tooling raises alerts that people have to triage rather than blocking everything by itself, and supervisors look at prevention, response and recovery alongside detection.

practicePrompt.question: A bank backs up its data every night to another server inside the same internal network, with separate access rights. Ransomware gets in. What is the problem?
options: Same network means the backup is encrypted at the same time as the original
Nightly backups are too infrequent; real-time replication is what is needed
Separate access rights are too weak and two-factor authentication is needed
The backup server needs more storage capacity than the primary one has
practicePrompt.explanation: Modern ransomware seeks out and encrypts the backups first, because they are the one thing that would let the victim avoid paying. Sitting on the same network means it can reach them, and separate access rights only slow it down rather than stopping it - an attacker already inside the network has time to escalate. Backups must be SEGREGATED from the main network, offline or write-once. Increasing the frequency of backups into that same location helps nothing: it just produces more copies to be encrypted together, and that is why recovery is treated as the equal of prevention.

keyTakeaways: Cyber has an adaptive adversary, so models built on historical frequency are especially weak
Least privilege does not stop an intrusion; it limits how far the damage spreads afterwards
Backups have to be segregated from the main network or they are encrypted alongside it
Outsourcing transfers the activity but never transfers the responsibility

summary.keyIdea: Recovery matters as much as prevention, because the realistic assumption is that an incident will happen sooner or later
summary.commonMistake: Spending almost the whole security budget on prevention and leaving detection, response and recovery thin
summary.action: For each critical system, ask: if it were compromised today, how long until we noticed and how long until it was restored

application.title: Apply it to yourself
application.message: Least privilege and segregated backups work for personal data too: does your main email account share a password with any other service, and does the backup of your photos sit in the same place as the originals?
application.secondary: The same logic, only the scale differs.

sections.text: Of the seven operational risk event categories, cyber is the only one whose cause is an adversary with intent, who learns and who actively looks for your weak points.
Why historical statistics are weak here

For a natural disaster or a keying error, the mechanism generating the event does not respond to your defences, so past frequency is a reasonable guide. An attacker watches the defence you have just put up and switches to another route - the risk distribution shifts in step with your own efforts to defend.

items: Identify: know where the critical information assets are and who can reach them
Prevent: least privilege, network segmentation, timely patching, multi-factor authentication
Detect: monitor for anomalies, measure the mean time to detect an intrusion
Respond and recover: rehearsed playbooks, segregated backups that cannot be overwritten

sections.label: Recovery matters as much as prevention
sections.text: Security budgets tend to pile into prevention, when the realistic assumption has to be that an incident will happen sooner or later. Two questions decide the eventual size of the loss: how long until it is detected, and how long until operations are restored.
Why a backup strategy that survives a disk failure is useless against ransomware

Backups were designed against an incident with no intent: a disk fails, a data centre burns, someone deletes the wrong thing. In those scenarios the backup sits still and is always intact. Ransomware inverts that founding assumption - the attacker gets in first, stays a while, finds the backup system itself and encrypts or deletes it, and only then triggers the visible part. By the time the organisation knows it has been attacked, the way back was cut off some time ago.

sections.label: A consequence for design, not for budget
sections.text: Backups need at least one version that cannot be overwritten and is not permanently connected, and just as importantly: recovery from that version has to be rehearsed. Plenty of organisations hold an offline backup but have never attempted a full restore from it, so they do not know it takes days. The question to answer first is not whether the backup exists but how long recovery takes and how the organisation operates in the meantime.

The second thing that sets cyber apart from the other operational risk categories: it is concentrated. When hundreds of institutions rely on the same handful of cloud providers, the same market data vendor or a shared payment system, one incident touches all of them at once. A contingency plan written on the assumption that everyone else is operating normally will be wrong in exactly the most severe class of event.

lines: Perfect defence is an unreachable goal; fast recovery is a reachable one.
Next lesson: fraud - the event category with the highest loss per incident.
